01 Antidepressants · class card

TCAs

tricyclic antidepressants · amitriptyline · clomipramine · desipramine · doxepin · imipramine · nortriptyline · protriptyline

Practice
  1. 74-year-old woman started on amitriptyline for postherpetic neuralgia 2 weeks later: new confusion, dry mouth, constipation could not void this morning; bladder felt above the pubis pulse 104/min · pupils large · blood pressure steady on standing → Muscarinic receptor blockade → amitriptyline, the most anticholinergic tricyclic, blocks muscarinic receptors, so the mouth dries, the bowel and bladder stall, the pulse quickens and an older brain clouds; alpha-1 block would drop her pressure on standing, and H1 block would sedate
  2. 38-year-old man took imipramine for 2 years stopped it on his own 3 days ago now nausea, vomiting, sweating, headache, aching muscles, irritability, poor sleep temperature normal · pupils normal · reflexes normal, no clonus · no new drugs → Cholinergic rebound → the long muscarinic block ends at once, so cholinergic activity overshoots: nausea, vomiting, sweating, headache, muscle aches, irritability and insomnia; a slow taper prevents it; no drug was added and he has no clonus or fever
  3. 79-year-old man with painful diabetic neuropathy in both feet a low-dose tricyclic is planned benign prostatic hyperplasia with a slow stream; mild constipation electrocardiogram normal · potassium normal · no conduction disease · no glaucoma → Nortriptyline → nortriptyline and desipramine, the secondary amines, block muscarinic receptors least, so they are the tricyclics for an older adult; amitriptyline blocks them most, and doxepin, also a tertiary amine, is strongly anticholinergic and sedating
